text: Hot water freezes faster than cold water under certain conditions, a phenomenon known as the Mpemba effect, and scientists still don't fully understand why.
If you could fold a piece of paper 42 times, it would reach the Moon. Each fold doubles the thickness exponentially.
A single bolt of lightning contains enough energy to toast 100,000 slices of bread, reaching temperatures five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
India's C.V. Raman won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for discovering that light changes wavelength when scattered — the Raman Effect.
Glass is not a solid or a liquid — it's an amorphous solid, with molecules arranged like a liquid but moving extremely slowly.
Tu Youyou of China discovered artemisinin by studying ancient Chinese herbal texts, saving millions of lives from malaria — earning a Nobel Prize in 2015.
Hot water can freeze faster than cold water under certain conditions — the Mpemba effect, named after a Tanzanian student who noticed it in 1963.
Scientists in Japan have created ice that is almost perfectly transparent by growing it very slowly, eliminating air bubbles entirely.
The Higgs boson, discovered at CERN in 2012, gives other particles mass through the Higgs field — a discovery that completed the Standard Model of particle physics.
DNA was first identified in 1869 by Swiss chemist Friedrich Miescher, nearly a century before Watson and Crick described its double-helix structure.
Quantum entanglement allows two particles to instantly share information regardless of distance — Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance.'
The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second — a fixed constant used to define the meter itself since 1983.
Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, is 200 times stronger than steel yet nearly transparent.
The human genome contains approximately 3 billion base pairs of DNA, encoding around 20,000 protein-coding genes.
Absolute zero, −273.15°C, is the coldest possible temperature; at this point atoms have minimal thermal energy and quantum effects dominate.
Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.
Bose-Einstein condensate, a fifth state of matter first created in 1995, forms when atoms are cooled to near absolute zero and behave as a single quantum entity.
The first antibiotic, penicillin, was accidentally discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 when mold contaminated a petri dish and killed surrounding bacteria.
Light behaves as both a particle and a wave — a duality confirmed by the double-slit experiment, one of quantum mechanics' most famous demonstrations.
The Periodic Table was independently conceived by Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev and German chemist Lothar Meyer in 1869, both organizing elements by atomic weight.
Photosynthesis converts about 1% of sunlight into chemical energy, yet it produces all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere and underpins almost all food chains.
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum because it requires a medium of molecules to carry pressure waves — unlike light, which needs no medium at all.
Einstein's E=mc² shows that mass and energy are interchangeable, with the speed of light squared as the conversion factor — a tiny mass yields enormous energy.
The CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, earned the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its precision in cutting DNA.
The second law of thermodynamics states that entropy — the measure of disorder in a system — always increases over time in an isolated system.
Neurons in the human brain transmit electrical signals at speeds up to 120 meters per second, faster than many race cars on a track.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography image of DNA, known as Photo 51, was pivotal in revealing the double-helix structure in 1953.
A neutron star packs more mass than our Sun into a sphere roughly 20 km across, making it so dense a teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tonnes.
The Doppler effect explains why an ambulance siren sounds higher-pitched as it approaches and lower-pitched as it moves away, due to compression and stretching of sound waves.
CERN's Large Hadron Collider accelerates protons to 99.9999991% of the speed of light — making it the largest and most complex machine ever built.
Helium, the second most abundant element in the universe, was discovered in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 before it was found on Earth.
The placebo effect is so powerful that even patients told they are receiving a placebo still show measurable clinical improvement in some conditions.
Carbon nanotubes are 100 times stronger than steel at one-sixth the weight, and their electrical conductivity rivals copper.
The human body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, each running thousands of chemical reactions every second to sustain life.
Bernoulli's principle explains why airplane wings generate lift: faster airflow over the curved top surface creates lower pressure than the slower flow beneath.
Tardigrades, eight-legged microscopic animals, can survive the vacuum of space, extreme radiation, and temperatures from −272°C to 150°C.
The uncertainty principle, formulated by Werner Heisenberg in 1927, states that you cannot simultaneously know both the exact position and momentum of a particle.
Mitochondria — the cell's 'power plants' — have their own DNA separate from the cell nucleus, evidence that they were once free-living bacteria absorbed by larger cells.
The first gravitational waves were detected by LIGO in September 2015, confirming a key prediction of Einstein's general theory of relativity made 100 years earlier.
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, an Indian astrophysicist, calculated the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf star in 1930 — work for which he won the Nobel Prize in 1983.
Superconductors conduct electricity with zero resistance when cooled below a critical temperature, enabling powerful magnets in MRI machines and particle accelerators.
Mendel's pea plant experiments, conducted in the 1860s, laid the groundwork for genetics — yet his work was ignored for 35 years before being rediscovered.
The laser — Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation — was first operated by Theodore Maiman in 1960 using a synthetic ruby crystal.
Water is one of the very few substances that expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats — a property critical for aquatic life surviving winters.
CRISPR exists in nature as a bacterial immune system: bacteria store fragments of virus DNA to recognize and destroy those viruses if they attack again.
The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, entered interstellar space in 2012 and remains the most distant human-made object ever, over 23 billion kilometres from Earth.
Ohm's Law states that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance (V = IR), a fundamental relationship underpinning all electrical circuit design.
Scanning tunnelling microscopy, invented in 1981 by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, allows scientists to image individual atoms on a surface — earning them the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The Milky Way contains between 200 and 400 billion stars, and astronomers estimate there are roughly two trillion galaxies in the observable universe.
Nils Bohr's model of the atom (1913) proposed electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels — still the basis of how students first learn atomic structure.
The ozone layer absorbs 97–99% of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation; its depletion by CFCs was so severe that the 1987 Montreal Protocol banned those chemicals globally.
The prion — an infectious misfolded protein — was discovered by Stanley Prusiner, earning him the 1997 Nobel Prize; prions cause diseases like BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob.
Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the theory of evolution by natural selection, presenting their findings jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.
Quantum tunnelling allows particles to pass through energy barriers they classically should not be able to cross — the mechanism powering nuclear fusion in the Sun.
The first element synthesised in a laboratory was technetium in 1937, filling gap 43 in the Periodic Table as the lightest element with no stable isotopes.
The Krebs cycle, discovered by Hans Krebs in 1937, is the central metabolic pathway in cells that extracts energy from nutrients to power life.
Sonar, used by bats and dolphins as echolocation, works by emitting sound pulses and listening for echoes — a biological application of acoustic wave physics.
The first image of a black hole was published in 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration, showing the supermassive black hole in galaxy M87.
Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a semi-permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to higher, driving nutrient uptake in plant roots.
Newton's third law — for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction — is why rockets work: exhaust gases pushing downward propel the rocket upward.
Shinya Yamanaka of Japan showed in 2006 that adult cells can be reprogrammed into stem cells (iPSCs) by introducing just four genes, earning the 2012 Nobel Prize.
Polarised light occurs when light waves vibrate in only one plane; polarising filters are used in sunglasses to cut glare by blocking horizontally polarised reflections.
The Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, was used in 1987 to observe Supernova 1987A — the first naked-eye supernova since 1604.
Catalysts speed up chemical reactions without being consumed; enzymes are biological catalysts that can accelerate reactions by a factor of up to 10 million.
Fractal geometry, developed by Benoît Mandelbrot in the 1970s, describes self-similar patterns found in coastlines, snowflakes, and even blood vessel networks.
The electric eel (Electrophorus electricus) can generate shocks up to 860 volts — enough to stun a horse — using specialised electrocyte cells in its body.
The Hall effect, discovered in 1879, describes how a magnetic field deflects current in a conductor sideways; the quantum Hall effect earned Klaus von Klitzing the 1985 Nobel Prize.
Ada Yonath of Israel determined the atomic structure of the ribosome using X-ray crystallography, sharing the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Plate tectonics theory, proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 and confirmed in the 1960s, explains how continents drift on molten rock at about the speed fingernails grow.
Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀), a soccer-ball-shaped molecule of 60 carbon atoms, was discovered in 1985 and its creators shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 failed to detect the hypothetical 'aether' medium for light, ultimately paving the way for Einstein's special relativity.
The average cloud weighs approximately 500 million kilograms, yet stays aloft because water droplets are so tiny that updrafts easily support them.
The first full sequence of the human genome was completed in 2003, but as of 2022 scientists published the truly complete genome including all repetitive regions for the first time.
Electromagnetic induction — discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831 — is the principle behind every electrical generator and transformer in the world.
MRNA vaccines work by instructing cells to produce a harmless viral protein that trains the immune system — the technology existed for decades before COVID-19.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for modifications to mRNA that made vaccines safe and effective in humans.
Archimedes' principle states that any object fully or partially submerged in fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces.
Bioluminescence — light produced by living organisms — occurs in over 80% of deep-sea creatures, used for attracting prey, finding mates, and camouflage.
At the quantum level, the vacuum of space is never truly empty — virtual particles constantly pop in and out of existence, a phenomenon confirmed by the Casimir effect.
The element francium is so unstable that at any given time, fewer than 30 grams of it exist naturally in the entire Earth's crust.
Stanley Miller's 1953 experiment showed that amino acids — life's building blocks — can form spontaneously from simple chemicals and simulated lightning.
Spiders produce silk that is, weight for weight, stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar — materials scientists are still trying to replicate it synthetically.
Abdus Salam of Pakistan shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for unifying electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force into the electroweak theory.
Black phosphorus, a layered semiconductor discovered in 1914, reemerged as a promising 2D material for electronics after graphene's success in the 2010s.
The theory of special relativity predicts time dilation: a clock moving at high speed ticks more slowly than a stationary one — confirmed by GPS satellites needing daily corrections.
The microbiome of the human gut contains about 100 trillion bacteria — roughly equal to the number of human cells — and influences immunity, metabolism, and mood.
The Nobel Prize-winning discovery of X-rays by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895 transformed medicine almost overnight, enabling doctors to see inside the body without surgery.
Superfluids, like liquid helium below 2.17 K, flow with zero viscosity and can climb up the walls of their container in a phenomenon called the fountain effect.
Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10²³) defines the number of units in one mole of any substance — a quantity so large that a mole of sand grains would cover Earth's surface one metre deep.
George Washington Carver, an African-American scientist, revolutionised Southern US agriculture by developing hundreds of products from peanuts, sweet potatoes, and soybeans.
Epigenetics studies heritable changes in gene expression that don't involve DNA sequence changes — diet, stress, and environment can alter which genes are switched on.
The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two identical fermions (such as electrons) can simultaneously occupy the same quantum state, which explains why matter has volume.
Mangrove forests store carbon up to four times more efficiently per hectare than tropical rainforests, making them crucial allies against climate change.
Piezoelectricity — the ability of certain crystals to generate voltage when compressed — was discovered by Pierre and Jacques Curie in 1880 and now powers quartz clocks and lighters.
The speed of sound in air at sea level is approximately 343 m/s, but sound travels nearly four times faster in water and fifteen times faster in steel.
Exoplanets — planets orbiting other stars — were first confirmed in 1992; by 2025 over 5,700 had been discovered, with thousands more candidates awaiting confirmation.
The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation, deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern, shaping weather systems.
The human eye can detect a single photon of light in total darkness — our visual system is exquisitely sensitive right down to the quantum limit.
The ocean covers over 70% of Earth's surface but humans have explored less than 20% of it; more of the Moon's surface has been mapped than the ocean floor.
Ferromagnetism — why iron is magnetic — arises when unpaired electron spins in a material align in the same direction, creating a net magnetic field.
Lise Meitner, an Austrian-Swedish physicist, co-discovered nuclear fission in 1938 with Otto Hahn; despite her pivotal role, only Hahn received the Nobel Prize.
Titanium is as strong as steel but 45% lighter, highly resistant to corrosion, and biocompatible — making it the preferred metal for medical implants and aircraft.
Telomeres, the protective caps on chromosome ends, shorten with each cell division and their length is linked to cellular ageing — a discovery that earned the 2009 Nobel Prize.
Non-Newtonian fluids like cornstarch and water (oobleck) become rigid under sudden impact but flow like a liquid when stressed slowly — a property rooted in polymer physics.
The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, can observe galaxies formed less than 400 million years after the Big Bang using infrared light.
Max Planck's discovery in 1900 that energy is emitted in discrete packets called quanta — not continuously — launched quantum mechanics and modern physics.
Metamaterials can bend light backwards around an object, effectively creating an 'invisibility cloak' for certain wavelengths by exploiting negative refractive index.
The photoelectric effect — light ejecting electrons from metal surfaces — was explained by Einstein in 1905, earning him the Nobel Prize and establishing light's particle nature.
Rosalyn Yalow, who won the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology, developed radioimmunoassay — a technique to measure trace amounts of hormones in blood using radioactive tracers.
Tectonic plates move at roughly 2–10 cm per year; the Atlantic Ocean grows by about the width of a human hand annually as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads.
The hydra, a freshwater organism, appears to be biologically immortal: it continuously replaces its cells and shows no signs of ageing under laboratory conditions.
The neutrino, nearly massless and electrically neutral, can pass through a light-year of lead with only a 50% chance of being stopped — trillions pass through your body every second.
Chien-Shiung Wu's 1956 experiment proved that parity — mirror symmetry — is violated in weak nuclear interactions, overturning a foundational assumption in physics.
Crystallography determined the structure of over 150,000 biological molecules, including insulin, haemoglobin, and DNA, transforming drug design.
The Cambrian Explosion, roughly 538 million years ago, saw most major animal body plans appear in the fossil record within about 25 million years — a blink in geological time.
Surface tension, the cohesive force among water molecules at a liquid's surface, is strong enough to let insects like water striders walk on water.
Photonic crystals — periodic nanostructures that manipulate light — give butterfly wings and opals their iridescent colours without any pigment.
The James-Stein estimator, introduced in 1961, showed that the ordinary least-squares estimate is inadmissible in three or more dimensions — a shocking result in statistics.
Radiocarbon dating, developed by Willard Libby in the late 1940s, uses the known decay rate of carbon-14 to date organic materials up to about 50,000 years old.
Wormholes are theoretical tunnels through spacetime permitted by Einstein's equations; none have been observed, but they remain an active area of theoretical physics.
The Scoville scale measures chilli heat by the concentration of capsaicin; pure capsaicin scores 16 million Scoville units — detectable by humans at 1 part per 11 million.
The Chandrayaan-3 mission made India only the fourth country to land on the Moon in August 2023 and the first to land near the lunar south pole.
Chimpanzees share approximately 98.7% of their DNA with humans — more genetically similar to us than they are to gorillas.
Interferometry combines waves from multiple telescopes to achieve the resolution of one enormous dish; it enabled the first black-hole image by linking radio telescopes across Earth.
The sodium-potassium pump in cell membranes moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per cycle, consuming about one-third of the body's total ATP energy.
The discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson provided strong evidence for the Big Bang theory.
The element osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, at 22,590 kg/m³ — a cube of osmium the size of a tennis ball would weigh about 27 kg.
Tokamak fusion reactors confine plasma with powerful magnetic fields; in 2022, the NIF achieved fusion ignition — releasing more energy than the lasers delivered to the target.
Biomimicry draws engineering inspiration from nature; Velcro was invented after George de Mestral studied how burr hooks clung to his dog's fur under a microscope.
In 1969, Har Gobind Khorana — an Indian-American biochemist — shared the Nobel Prize for interpreting the genetic code and its role in protein synthesis.
Salt (NaCl) lowers water's freezing point through freezing-point depression — the basis for spreading salt on icy roads, effective down to about −9°C.
Quantum computing uses qubits that can exist in superpositions of 0 and 1 simultaneously, potentially solving certain problems exponentially faster than classical computers.
Messenger RNA was discovered in 1960 by Sydney Brenner and François Jacob; it carries genetic instructions from DNA to ribosomes where proteins are assembled.
The placebo effect has a counterpart: the nocebo effect, where negative expectations cause real, measurable harm — even from inert treatments.
Sonoluminescence occurs when a tiny air bubble in water is vibrated by ultrasound and collapses so violently that it briefly emits light and reaches temperatures of ~20,000 K.
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova explosion recorded by Chinese and Arab astronomers in 1054 AD; at its centre spins a pulsar 30 times per second.
The skin is the body's largest organ, covering about 1.7 m² in an adult; it regenerates completely approximately every 27 days.
Quantum decoherence explains why quantum superpositions vanish in everyday objects: interactions with the environment destroy quantum effects almost instantaneously.
Ammonia synthesis via the Haber-Bosch process, developed in 1909, produces the nitrogen fertilisers that sustain roughly half of all food grown on Earth today.
Satyendra Nath Bose collaborated with Einstein in the 1920s to develop Bose-Einstein statistics, leading to the prediction of the Bose-Einstein condensate.
The electric charge of a single electron is −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, one of the fundamental constants of nature measured to extraordinary precision by NIST.
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is 101,325 Pa (1 atm), enough force to support a column of mercury 760 mm tall — first demonstrated by Evangelista Torricelli in 1643.
The deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystem, discovered in 1977, showed life could thrive without sunlight — powered by chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis.
Silicon carbide, a ceramic semiconductor, can operate at temperatures above 600°C and is being integrated into next-generation power electronics and electric vehicles.
The Mpemba effect aside, water has dozens of known anomalies including a density maximum at 4°C — explaining why lakes freeze from the top down and aquatic life survives winters.
The Voyager Golden Record, sent into space in 1977, contains greetings in 55 languages, 116 images, and music including works by Bach and Chuck Berry.
The Compton effect, observed in 1923, showed X-rays scattering off electrons with reduced energy — direct evidence that photons carry momentum like particles.
The human liver performs over 500 distinct biochemical functions, including detoxification, protein synthesis, and producing bile for digestion.
Aerogel, the lightest solid material ever made (as low as 1 mg/cm³), is 99.8% air and an extraordinary thermal insulator — used in NASA Mars rovers.
Brain-computer interfaces, first demonstrated by Miguel Nicolelis in the 1990s, have enabled paralysed patients to control robotic limbs using thought alone.
Fourier analysis, developed by Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier around 1822, decomposes any waveform into a sum of sine waves — foundational in music, optics, and signal processing.
The Giant Impact Hypothesis proposes the Moon formed when a Mars-sized body called Theia collided with early Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
Chirality in chemistry describes molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images; many pharmaceuticals are chiral, with one form therapeutic and the other potentially harmful.
The naked mole rat is extraordinarily resistant to cancer and pain, and can survive up to 18 minutes without oxygen — making it a key model in longevity research.
Plasma, the fourth state of matter, makes up more than 99% of the visible universe including stars, nebulae, and the solar wind streaming past Earth.
Hawking radiation, predicted theoretically by Stephen Hawking in 1974, proposes that black holes slowly evaporate by emitting particles due to quantum effects near the event horizon.
The electric eel can sense weak electric fields in water to locate prey in murky conditions — a sense called electroreception, shared by sharks and some fish.
Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) describes the strong nuclear force that binds quarks into protons and neutrons using 'colour charge' carried by gluons.
Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element; at any moment, less than 28 grams exists in Earth's crust due to its extremely short half-life.
Louis Pasteur's germ theory — developed in the 1860s — proved that microorganisms cause disease, overturning the centuries-old miasma theory and founding modern medicine.
The total length of DNA in a single human cell, if stretched out, would be about 2 metres; laid end to end from all your cells it would reach the Sun and back about 300 times.
The concept of enthalpy underpins all calorimetry; the calories listed on food labels represent the heat released when that food is fully combusted in a calorimeter.
The LIGO-Virgo detectors are so sensitive they can measure a displacement 10,000 times smaller than a proton — needed to detect gravitational waves stretching spacetime.
Bats navigate using ultrasound at frequencies up to 200 kHz — far beyond the 20 kHz upper limit of human hearing — allowing submillimetre precision in the dark.
The continental shelf — the shallow sea floor bordering continents — covers only 7% of the ocean's area yet contains 90% of all marine species.
In 1958 Jagdish Chandra Bose was posthumously recognised for his pioneering work on radio waves and plant physiology — his 1890s crescograph measured plant growth with extraordinary precision.
The Stern-Gerlach experiment in 1922 directly demonstrated electron spin by splitting a beam of silver atoms in two when passed through an inhomogeneous magnetic field.
Viruses are not considered alive because they cannot reproduce independently, have no metabolism, and rely entirely on a host cell's machinery to replicate.
The Planck length (1.616 × 10⁻³⁵ m) is the smallest meaningful length in physics; below it, quantum effects on spacetime make current physics break down.
Phase-contrast microscopy, developed by Frits Zernike and recognised with the 1953 Nobel Prize, allowed biologists to observe living, unstained cells for the first time.
The highest temperature ever achieved in a laboratory is about 4 trillion °C, created at CERN's ALICE detector by colliding lead ions — briefly hotter than the early universe.
Bioplastics made from corn starch or sugarcane can decompose in months rather than centuries, potentially replacing petroleum-based plastics in packaging.
The butterfly effect, coined by Edward Lorenz, describes how tiny changes in initial conditions (like a butterfly flapping its wings) can drastically alter complex systems like weather.
Chemiluminescence is the emission of light from a chemical reaction without heat; it powers glow sticks and the bioluminescence of fireflies.
RNA interference (RNAi), discovered by Andrew Fire and Craig Mello in 1998, allows small RNA molecules to silence specific genes — earning the 2006 Nobel Prize.
The deepest point on Earth, Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, reaches 10,935 metres below sea level — deep enough to submerge Mount Everest with 2 km to spare.
Ernest Rutherford's 1911 gold-foil experiment revealed the atomic nucleus: most alpha particles passed straight through, but a few bounced back — proving atoms are mostly empty space.
The mass of the universe is estimated at about 10⁵³ kg, with ordinary matter making up just 5%; the rest is dark matter (27%) and dark energy (68%).
Robert Boyle's 1662 gas law shows that at constant temperature the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional — one of the foundational gas laws.
Müller-Lyer illusion demonstrates that perception differs from reality: two identical line segments appear different lengths depending on the direction of arrowheads at their ends.
The first synthetic polymer, Bakelite, was invented by Leo Baekeland in 1907 and launched the modern plastics industry — still used today in electrical insulators.
ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter Array in Chile, consists of 66 radio telescopes working together and can image discs of gas and dust around distant stars in extraordinary detail.
Fluorescence occurs when a molecule absorbs high-energy UV light and re-emits lower-energy visible light almost instantly — the basis of fluorescent lamps and biological markers.
The endosymbiotic theory, championed by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s, proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts in eukaryotic cells were once independent bacteria.
Wilson's cloud chamber (1911) made ionising particles visible for the first time by allowing them to leave tracks of condensed water vapour — winning the 1927 Nobel Prize.
The discovery of neon (1898), xenon, krypton, and argon filled in the last group of the Periodic Table and earned William Ramsay the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The surface of a soap bubble is only about 10 nanometres thick — a few hundred molecules — yet it can persist for hours thanks to surface tension and evaporation control.
Horizontal gene transfer allows bacteria to swap genetic material across species — a major driver of antibiotic resistance spreading between unrelated bacteria.
Tungsten has the highest melting point of all elements at 3,422°C, which is why it is used as the filament in incandescent light bulbs.
The cochlea in the human ear, a fluid-filled spiral, separates sounds by frequency along its length — high-pitched sounds at the base, low-pitched at the apex.
Phytoplankton produce approximately half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis — making the ocean as important as all terrestrial forests combined.
The Zeeman effect — the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field — was discovered in 1896 and provided the first evidence that atoms contain charged particles.
Biomineralisation allows organisms such as mussels, corals, and diatoms to grow structures like shells and bones by precisely controlling crystallisation of minerals.
In 1989, IBM researchers spelled 'IBM' using 35 individual xenon atoms manipulated with a scanning tunnelling microscope — the first ever atomic-scale writing.
The gravitational constant G (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²) is the least precisely known fundamental constant in physics, measured to only 5 significant figures with confidence.
In 2016, AlphaFold from DeepMind solved the 50-year-old protein-folding problem; by 2022 it had predicted the 3D structure of nearly every known protein, transforming biology.
Mercury is liquid at room temperature because relativistic effects shrink its 6s electron orbitals, weakening metallic bonding enough that melting requires very little energy.
Srinivasa Ramanujan, a self-taught Indian mathematician, independently discovered thousands of formulas in number theory that professional mathematicians had never seen.
Zinc is essential for over 300 enzymatic reactions in the human body; deficiency affects more than 2 billion people worldwide and impairs immune function and growth.
The International Space Station orbits Earth at about 400 km altitude travelling at 7.66 km/s, completing one full orbit every 92 minutes.
The brain uses about 20% of the body's total energy despite comprising only 2% of its mass — largely because neurons require constant ion pumping to maintain electrical potential.
Diamond is the hardest natural substance (10 on the Mohs scale) but is metastable at room temperature — graphite, not diamond, is the most stable form of carbon.
Magnetotactic bacteria contain chains of iron-oxide nanoparticles called magnetosomes and use them as a biological compass to navigate along Earth's magnetic field lines.
The first observation of a quasicrystal — an atomic structure with five-fold symmetry previously considered impossible — earned Dan Shechtman the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The power of a hurricane is estimated at about 10 petawatts from its water-cycle processes — equivalent to half the world's total electricity generation capacity.
High-temperature superconductivity was discovered in copper-oxide ceramics in 1986 by Bednorz and Müller, shattering the previous record by 12 K and winning a Nobel Prize in 1987.
The number of possible games of chess exceeds 10¹²⁰ — more than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe — making exhaustive computation impossible.
Yuki Hayashi and colleagues demonstrated in 2024 that a room-temperature ambient-pressure superconductor candidate would transform energy transmission — research still under intense global scrutiny.
Superconductors expel magnetic fields entirely when cooled below their critical temperature — a phenomenon called the Meissner effect, discovered in 1933 by Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld.
Liquid helium-4 becomes a superfluid below 2.17 K (the lambda point), flowing with zero viscosity and even climbing up container walls in defiance of gravity.
Plasma physics gave birth to tokamak reactors: doughnut-shaped magnetic confinement chambers that heat hydrogen isotopes to 150 million °C — ten times hotter than the Sun's core.
Spectroscopy — splitting light into its component wavelengths — allowed astronomers to identify helium in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, two decades before it was isolated on Earth.
X-ray crystallography, pioneered by William and Lawrence Bragg in 1913, works by firing X-rays at a crystal and measuring how they diffract to reconstruct atomic positions.
Mass spectrometry ionises molecules and sorts them by their mass-to-charge ratio; modern instruments can detect a single molecule of a compound at parts-per-quadrillion concentration.
The transmission electron microscope (TEM) accelerates electrons to near light speed and can resolve individual atoms, achieving sub-ångström resolution far beyond optical microscopes.
Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 by accident: uranium salts sitting on unexposed photographic plates in a dark drawer still fogged them, revealing spontaneous radiation.
Nuclear fission of one kilogram of uranium-235 releases energy equivalent to burning about 3,000 tonnes of coal — a factor of roughly 3 million times more energy per unit mass.
Antimatter was predicted by Paul Dirac's 1928 equation and confirmed when Carl Anderson observed the positron in 1932 — the first antiparticle ever detected.
When a particle meets its antiparticle they annihilate completely, converting all their mass into energy — proton-antiproton annihilation produces mostly pions and photons.
Neutrinos are so weakly interacting that a neutrino can travel through a light-year of solid lead with only a 50% chance of being stopped — about 10²⁵ times more penetrating than a photon.

The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald for proving neutrinos oscillate between three flavours — proving they have mass, which the Standard Model originally assumed was zero.

Muons are essentially heavy electrons — 207 times more massive — that rain down from cosmic-ray interactions in the upper atmosphere at a rate of about one per square centimetre per minute at sea level.
Quarks were proposed by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig in 1964; the top quark — the heaviest at 173 GeV/c² — was not confirmed until 1995 at Fermilab.
String theory proposes that fundamental particles are one-dimensional vibrating strings; different vibration modes produce different particles, requiring at least 10 spacetime dimensions.
M-theory, a unifying extension of the five string theories, requires 11 spacetime dimensions and was proposed by Edward Witten in 1995 at a landmark string theory conference.

Chaos theory shows that tiny differences in initial conditions produce wildly different outcomes; Edward Lorenz discovered this in 1961 when truncating a weather simulation to three decimal places completely changed the forecast.
The second law of thermodynamics states that entropy — the measure of disorder — in a closed system never decreases; this arrow of time is one of physics' most profound asymmetries.
A phase transition occurs when matter changes state — ice melting into water is first-order, while the ferromagnetic transition in iron at its Curie point is second-order, with no latent heat.
The first Bose-Einstein condensate was created in 1995 by Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman at NIST, cooling rubidium-87 atoms to 170 nanokelvin — earning the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Ferrofluids are liquids that become strongly magnetised in the presence of a magnetic field; invented at NASA in the 1960s, they are used in loudspeakers, hard-drive seals, and MRI contrast agents.

Piezoelectricity — electricity generated by mechanical stress — was discovered by Pierre and Jacques Curie in 1880; today piezoelectric crystals power everything from gas lighters to ultrasound scanners.

Tribology — the science of friction, lubrication, and wear — estimates that 23% of the world's energy consumption is lost to friction, with better tribology potentially saving hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
The Geiger-Müller tube, invented in 1908 and refined in 1928, detects ionising radiation by measuring electrical pulses caused by radiation ionising gas inside a sealed tube.
The scanning tunnelling microscope (STM), invented by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in 1981, images surfaces atom by atom using quantum tunnelling — earning the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Citizen science project Galaxy Zoo, launched in 2007, enlisted 150,000 volunteers to classify over a million galaxy images — discovering unusual objects no automated algorithm had flagged.
The Michelson-Morley experiment in 1887 tried to detect Earth's motion through the hypothetical 'aether' and found nothing — a null result that paved the way for Einstein's special relativity.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes; within weeks the discovery spread worldwide and doctors were using X-ray images to see inside patients.

The Hall effect, discovered by Edwin Hall in 1879, produces a voltage perpendicular to both current flow and an applied magnetic field — now the basis of magnetic field sensors used in car wheel-speed detectors.

The quantum Hall effect, discovered in 1980 by Klaus von Klitzing, shows that electrical resistance in 2D materials at low temperatures takes only exact integer multiples of h/e² — a perfect natural standard of resistance.
Spontaneous symmetry breaking — where a system's lowest-energy state lacks the full symmetry of its governing equations — underlies both the Higgs mechanism and the formation of snowflake patterns.

The Josephson effect — quantum tunnelling of Cooper pairs through a thin insulating barrier between two superconductors — produces an oscillating current with a frequency so precise it defines the international voltage standard.
Rayleigh scattering — the scattering of light by particles far smaller than its wavelength — explains why the sky is blue: shorter blue wavelengths scatter roughly 10 times more than red ones.
The photoelectric effect — that light below a threshold frequency cannot eject electrons regardless of intensity — was explained by Einstein in 1905 and earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Cooper pairs — bound electron pairs that form in superconductors at low temperatures — travel through a crystal lattice with zero electrical resistance, explained by the BCS theory of 1957.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy probes atomic nuclei by placing them in a strong magnetic field and measuring their radio-frequency absorptions — the same physics that underlies MRI scanners.

Raman spectroscopy, discovered by C.V. Raman in 1928, reveals molecular vibrations by analysing light scattered inelastically; it can identify a molecule from a single cell and won Raman the 1930 Nobel Prize.

The Mössbauer effect — recoil-free gamma-ray emission and absorption by atomic nuclei in solids — allowed the first laboratory measurement of gravitational redshift, confirming general relativity in 1960.
Particle accelerators have grown from Ernest Lawrence's 4-inch cyclotron in 1930 to CERN's Large Hadron Collider — 27 km in circumference — accelerating protons to 99.9999991% of the speed of light.

The strange metal state — found in many high-temperature superconductors above their critical temperature — has electrical resistance that scales linearly with temperature, defying conventional metal theory.
The isotope effect in superconductors — where heavier isotopes lower the critical temperature — was crucial evidence for the phonon-mediated BCS mechanism of conventional superconductivity.
Sonoluminescence — the emission of a flash of light when a sound-driven bubble collapses in a liquid — produces temperatures estimated at 10,000–20,000 K inside the collapsing bubble.
The Mpemba effect — sometimes hot water freezes faster than cold water — was described to physicist Denis Osborne by a Tanzanian student, Erasto Mpemba, in 1963; the mechanism is still debated.
The Hubble Ultra Deep Field image, assembled from 800 exposures totalling 11.3 days, revealed approximately 10,000 galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
Failed attempts to synthesise dyes from aniline led William Perkin in 1856 to accidentally create mauveine — the first synthetic dye — launching the entire synthetic chemistry industry.
Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) was discovered accidentally by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938 when a cylinder of refrigerant gas unexpectedly polymerised overnight in a cold laboratory.
Post-it Notes were invented because Spencer Silver at 3M failed to make a strong adhesive in 1968; six years later a colleague used the weak adhesive to stop bookmarks falling from his hymn book.
Saccharin was discovered in 1879 when chemist Constantin Fahlberg forgot to wash his hands after working with coal-tar derivatives and found his bread unusually sweet at dinner.
The citizen science project SETI@home, active from 1999 to 2020, used idle processing power on millions of home computers to search for extraterrestrial signals in radio telescope data.

Folding@home, launched in 2000, lets volunteers donate idle computer time to simulate protein folding; during the COVID-19 pandemic it became the world's most powerful distributed computing system at over 2.4 exaflops.
The Lorenz attractor — the butterfly-shaped solution to three chaotic differential equations — shows how deterministic systems can produce infinitely complex, non-repeating trajectories.
Percolation theory describes how fluids move through porous media and explains phase transitions in networks; it predicts the precise moment a random network becomes fully connected.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction Photo 51, taken in 1952, showed the helical structure of DNA and was pivotal to Watson and Crick constructing their double-helix model in 1953.

Chirped pulse amplification — stretching, amplifying, then recompressing laser pulses to achieve enormous peak powers without destroying the amplifier — earned Donna Strickland and Gérard Mourou the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The Casimir effect — an attractive force between uncharged metal plates in a vacuum due to quantum fluctuations in the electromagnetic field — was measured directly for the first time in 1997.

Gravitational lensing — predicted by Einstein — bends light from distant galaxies around massive galaxy clusters, creating arcs, Einstein rings, and allowing the mass of invisible dark matter to be mapped.
The tau neutrino, the third neutrino flavour, was the last Standard Model particle confirmed before the Higgs boson, detected by the DONUT experiment at Fermilab in 2000.
Muon tomography uses cosmic-ray muons passing through dense materials to image the interiors of volcanoes, nuclear reactors, and even the Great Pyramid — revealing a hidden chamber in 2017.
Pair production — the creation of a particle–antiparticle pair from a high-energy photon near a nucleus — is a direct demonstration of E = mc²; it requires at least 1.022 MeV of energy.
Magnetic monopoles — isolated north or south magnetic poles — are predicted by Grand Unified Theories but have never been observed, despite extensive searches including CERN's MoEDAL detector.
Topological insulators are materials that conduct electricity only on their surface while remaining insulating in the interior — a quantum phase of matter confirmed experimentally in 2007.

René-Just Haüy founded crystallography in the 1780s after dropping a friend's calcite crystal and noticing that every fragment had the same geometric shape — leading him to the law of rational indices.
The time-of-flight mass spectrometer fires ions down a long tube; lighter ions reach the detector first, allowing precise mass measurements accurate to better than one part per million.

The focused ion beam (FIB) instrument uses a beam of gallium ions to sculpt materials at nanometre precision — both cutting sections for electron microscopy and depositing metal contacts on microchips.
Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) in a scanning electron microscope maps the crystallographic orientation of every grain in a polycrystalline material — revealing how metals deform and fail.

Synchrotron radiation — intense X-ray beams produced when electrons are bent in particle storage rings — is 10 billion times brighter than a hospital X-ray and is used to determine protein structures in minutes.
The decay chain of uranium-238 passes through 14 radioactive daughters before ending as stable lead-206, spanning half-lives from 4.5 billion years to 164 microseconds.
CP violation — the subtle asymmetry between matter and antimatter discovered in kaon decay in 1964 — is the leading candidate for explaining why the universe contains more matter than antimatter.
The Penrose tiling — a non-periodic tiling of the plane with five-fold symmetry discovered in 1974 — anticipated quasicrystals and shows that non-repeating structures can fill space perfectly.

The optical tweezer — a tightly focused laser beam that traps and moves microscopic objects using radiation pressure — was invented by Arthur Ashkin in the 1970s and used to study DNA mechanics, earning him the 2018 Nobel Prize.

Strange quarks, found in kaons and other 'strange' particles, decay via the weak force to up quarks; their anomalously long lifetime puzzled physicists in the 1950s and drove the development of the quark model.
The Cherenkov effect — a blue glow produced when a charged particle travels faster than light moves in that medium — is used in detectors like Super-Kamiokande to catch neutrinos and cosmic rays.

The fractional quantum Hall effect, discovered in 1982 at 1/3 and other fractional filling of Landau levels, revealed quasiparticles with fractional charge — a profoundly unexpected collective quantum phenomenon.

Cold fusion was claimed by Pons and Fleischmann in 1989 but failed to be replicated; it became a landmark case in the sociology of science about the dangers of rushing extraordinary claims without peer review.

George Ohm's 1827 law — that current through a conductor is proportional to voltage — was initially rejected by German academics as 'naked fantasy'; he was vindicated by the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1841.

Ignaz Semmelweis discovered in 1847 that handwashing dramatically reduced puerperal fever deaths in maternity wards, yet was ridiculed by the medical establishment and died in a psychiatric institution in 1865.
Stochastic resonance — adding a small amount of noise to a weak signal can make it detectable — explains how some neurons and sensory systems exploit background noise to enhance faint stimuli.
The Mpemba-like quantum effect — proposed in 2020 — suggests quantum systems can also cool faster from a hotter initial state under certain conditions, extending chaos into the quantum realm.
Solar neutrino problem: for decades, only a third of the predicted neutrinos from the Sun were detected; the resolution was neutrino oscillation — neutrinos were changing flavour en route to Earth.

The proton radius puzzle arose when muonic hydrogen measurements gave a proton radius 4% smaller than electron-based methods; the discrepancy sparked intense experimental effort and was partially resolved by 2019.

The anomalous magnetic dipole moment of the muon (g-2), measured with extraordinary precision at Fermilab, shows a tiny persistent deviation from Standard Model predictions — hinting at undiscovered physics.

Quantum entanglement allows two particles to share a quantum state such that measuring one instantly determines the other's state regardless of distance — confirmed by Bell test experiments closing all major loopholes by 2015.
Magnetically levitated (maglev) trains use superconducting coils to float the train above the track with no friction; the Japanese SCMaglev holds the world rail speed record at 603 km/h, set in 2015.

The Voyager 1 probe, launched in 1977, became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space in 2012; the confirmation required detecting a sudden change in the plasma environment around the spacecraft.
Ball lightning — floating luminous orbs seen during thunderstorms — remains scientifically unexplained; proposed mechanisms range from plasma vortices to microwave radiation trapped in air cavities.
Gamma-ray bursts are the most energetic explosions in the universe, releasing more energy in a few seconds than the Sun will emit in its entire 10-billion-year lifetime.
The r-process — rapid neutron capture in neutron star mergers — creates heavy elements like gold and platinum; the 2017 LIGO observation of merging neutron stars confirmed this origin directly.

Metamaterials with a negative refractive index bend light backwards and can theoretically produce a 'perfect lens' with resolution below the diffraction limit, first demonstrated by Sir John Pendry in 2000.
The butterfly effect was named by Edward Lorenz in 1972 in his talk 'Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?' — now the most famous metaphor in chaos theory.
The first X-ray CT scanner for clinical use was developed by Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI in 1972, a discovery inspired partly by his earlier work on Beatles album sales funding EMI's research labs.

Supersolid helium-4 — a state where a material is simultaneously crystalline solid and superfluid — was controversially reported in 2004 and has since been partially confirmed as a form of superfluidity of crystal defects.

Chaos in the asteroid belt is responsible for delivering meteorites to Earth; tiny gravitational nudges from Jupiter over millions of years push asteroids onto Earth-crossing orbits through chaotic resonance.

The Stern-Gerlach experiment of 1922 fired silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field and split the beam into two discrete bands, providing the first direct evidence of quantised angular momentum (spin).

The three-body problem — predicting the trajectories of three mutually gravitating bodies — has no general closed-form solution; even tiny measurement errors make long-term prediction impossible, a form of chaos.
Coulomb's law of electrostatic force, formulated in 1785, took the same inverse-square form as Newton's gravity — a formal similarity that later inspired unified gauge-field theories of all forces.

Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) used as MRI contrast agents can be targeted to cancer cells using antibody coatings, heating and destroying tumours when exposed to alternating magnetic fields.

The piezoelectric coefficient of lead zirconate titanate (PZT) is so high it is used in sonar transducers, atomic force microscope cantilevers, and precision nanopositioning stages that move sub-nanometre distances.

The Wiedemann-Franz law (1853) shows that good electrical conductors are also good thermal conductors; the ratio of thermal to electrical conductivity is proportional to temperature — a fundamental result explained by free-electron theory.

Chaos control — the technique of applying tiny, precisely timed perturbations to steer a chaotic system to a periodic orbit — was demonstrated in 1990 and is used to stabilise cardiac arrhythmias and laser outputs.

The photoelectric effect in solar cells converts photons directly into electricity; modern silicon cells achieve about 22% efficiency, while multi-junction concentrator cells exceed 47% in laboratory conditions.
The Pauli exclusion principle — that no two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state simultaneously — is responsible for the stability of matter: without it, atoms would collapse.
Phosphorescence differs from fluorescence in that excited electrons are trapped in a metastable state for milliseconds to hours before emitting light — the basis of glow-in-the-dark materials.

The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 was awarded for Bell inequality experiments to Aspect, Clauser, and Zeilinger, closing loopholes and definitively confirming quantum nonlocality over 'hidden variable' theories.

Entropy increases in isolated systems because there are overwhelmingly more disordered microstates than ordered ones; Boltzmann's formula S = k·ln(W) links macroscopic entropy to microscopic counting.

The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability — the rolling wave pattern at the boundary between two fluids moving at different speeds — creates the wavy cloud formations sometimes called 'Kelvin-Helmholtz clouds' in the atmosphere.

The Rayleigh-Bénard convection instability — where a layer of fluid heated from below develops organised hexagonal convection cells — is a paradigmatic example of self-organisation far from equilibrium.

The Standard Model of particle physics describes 17 fundamental particles and their interactions but excludes gravity; reconciling it with general relativity remains one of the greatest unsolved problems in physics.

Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained nuclear fission in January 1939 using the liquid-drop model; their paper coined the term 'fission' and was read at Princeton by a colleague who immediately told Einstein.

Dark matter interacts via gravity but not electromagnetism; the most compelling evidence is galaxy rotation curves — stars at all radii orbit at roughly the same speed rather than slowing at greater distances.

Vera Rubin's careful measurements of galaxy rotation curves in the 1970s provided some of the most compelling observational evidence for dark matter — work that was unjustly overlooked for a Nobel Prize.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scans exploit antimatter: a radiotracer emits positrons that annihilate with electrons, producing pairs of 511-keV gamma rays detected simultaneously by ring detectors.

Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) rapidly vitrifies proteins in liquid ethane, preserving their native shape without crystals; the 2017 Nobel Chemistry Prize recognised how it revolutionised structural biology.

Neutron stars spin up to 716 times per second (millisecond pulsars), beaming radio waves like a cosmic lighthouse; they are so dense that a teaspoon of neutron-star material would weigh about a billion tonnes.
Quark-gluon plasma — the state of matter microseconds after the Big Bang — was recreated at CERN's Large Hadron Collider by colliding lead nuclei; temperatures exceeded 5 trillion °C.
The discovery of the J/ψ meson simultaneously at Stanford and Brookhaven in November 1974 — 'The November Revolution' — confirmed the existence of the charm quark and the quark model itself.
Quantum tunnelling allows particles to cross energy barriers they classically cannot — it powers nuclear fusion in the Sun, alpha decay in radioactive nuclei, and flash memory in computers.

Magnons — quantised collective spin waves in magnetic materials — can transport information like electrons but generate far less heat; magnon-based 'magnonics' devices may underpin low-power future computers.

Electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy detects unpaired electrons by placing a sample in a magnetic field and sweeping microwave frequencies; it identifies free radicals in chemistry and biological systems.

Infrared spectroscopy identifies molecules by the frequencies at which they absorb infrared light, matching the natural vibration modes of their chemical bonds — a fingerprint technique central to forensic science and quality control.

Flow cytometry can analyse up to 100,000 cells per second by passing them single-file through laser beams, measuring size, granularity, and fluorescent labels — transforming immunology and cancer diagnostics.

The concept of temperature was only fully formalised by the zeroth law of thermodynamics — that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other — added to physics after the first, second, and third laws.
Absolute zero (0 K, −273.15 °C) is the temperature at which classical thermal motion would cease; the third law of thermodynamics states it is impossible to reach in a finite number of steps.
Rutherford's transmutation of nitrogen into oxygen by bombarding it with alpha particles in 1919 was the first artificial nuclear reaction — proving atoms could be deliberately transformed.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation, discovered accidentally by Penzias and Wilson in 1965 while tracking down noise in a communications antenna, is the afterglow of the Big Bang and earned them the 1978 Nobel Prize.

Fluorine is the most electronegative and most reactive element; it reacts violently with nearly every substance including glass, asbestos, and water — and even reacts explosively with xenon, a noble gas.
The Haber-Bosch process (1913) synthesises ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen; it now feeds roughly half the world's population but consumes about 1-2% of global energy.
Quantum dots are semiconductor nanocrystals whose emission colour is tuned purely by size — larger dots emit red, smaller emit blue — used in QLED TV screens and biological imaging.

Hysteresis in magnetic materials — where the magnetisation depends on history, not just the current applied field — is why permanent magnets retain magnetism and is exploited in magnetic recording and transformers.

The discovery that DNA is the genetic material came from Oswald Avery's 1944 transformation experiment, not Watson and Crick; Avery showed that purified DNA from dead bacteria could permanently transform living bacteria.

CRISPR-Cas9, adapted from bacterial immune systems, acts as molecular scissors that can cut DNA at precise locations; its discoverers Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins (opsins) to control individual neurons with millisecond precision using fibre-optic light pulses, allowing researchers to switch specific brain circuits on and off in living animals.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy probes how the internal resistance of batteries changes with frequency, revealing degradation mechanisms at the electrode-electrolyte interface — crucial for electric vehicle battery management.

Triboluminescence — light emitted when materials are crushed or broken — was first described by Francis Bacon in 1605; chewing Wint-O-Green Life Savers candy in the dark produces visible blue sparks from it.
Isotope tracing — replacing atoms with heavier isotopes like deuterium or carbon-13 and tracking them by mass spectrometry or NMR — mapped virtually all major metabolic pathways in the 20th century.

The Zeeman effect — the splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field, discovered in 1896 — provided early evidence for electron spin and remains a key astrophysical tool for measuring stellar magnetic field strengths.

The Stark effect — splitting of spectral lines by an electric field, discovered in 1913 — complements the Zeeman effect and is used to precisely control atomic transitions in quantum computing experiments.
The proton has an internal structure; deep inelastic scattering experiments at SLAC in 1968 revealed that it is not a point particle but contains hard, point-like constituents — the quarks.

The Coriolis effect deflects moving air masses to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern — driving the rotation of hurricanes counterclockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.

Helium-3, with two protons and one neutron, is a rare isotope critical for neutron detectors and dilution refrigerators that cool quantum computers to millikelvin temperatures; its global supply is limited to nuclear weapons stockpiles.

The proton-proton chain reaction powers the Sun, fusing four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus over a series of steps and releasing 26.7 MeV of energy — the source of virtually all life-sustaining sunlight on Earth.

Non-Newtonian fluids such as cornstarch in water (oobleck) act as solids under rapid stress and liquids otherwise — a property called shear thickening used in liquid body armour that hardens on impact.
The Wien displacement law states that the peak emission wavelength of a blackbody shifts inversely with temperature; it lets astronomers infer stellar surface temperatures from colour alone.
Negative temperature states — where adding energy reduces entropy — can occur in population-inverted quantum systems like laser gain media; these systems are hotter than any positive temperature.

Protein crystallisation for X-ray crystallography is often the hardest step; many proteins resist forming crystals, and the International Space Station has been used as a microgravity platform to grow better protein crystals.

Atomic clocks based on caesium-133 hyperfine transitions define the second and are accurate to one second in 300 million years; optical lattice clocks now reach 10⁻¹⁸ accuracy — one second in 30 billion years.
The anomalous expansion of water between 0 °C and 4 °C — where cooling water below 4 °C makes it less dense rather than denser — allows ice to float and aquatic life to survive frozen winters.

The electric field of a radio wave can be used to wirelessly transfer energy; WiTricity, a technology derived from MIT research in 2007, uses resonant inductive coupling to charge devices at distances of up to a metre.

Galvani's accidental discovery in the 1780s that frog legs twitched when touched by two different metals launched the science of bioelectricity and inspired Volta's invention of the first electrochemical battery.

Metamorphic rocks form under intense heat and pressure deep in Earth's crust; the mineral assemblages they contain act as geological pressure-temperature gauges, recording ancient tectonic conditions.

The Kibble balance (formerly the watt balance) uses electromagnetic force to precisely measure mass; since 2019 it has defined the kilogram in terms of Planck's constant, replacing the physical platinum-iridium prototype.

The gyroscope effect — a spinning object resists changes to its axis of rotation — explains precession in gyroscopes, tops, bicycles, and even the Earth, whose axis wobbles with a 26,000-year Milankovitch cycle.

The de Broglie hypothesis (1924) proposed that all matter has an associated wavelength λ = h/p; confirmed by electron diffraction experiments in 1927, it led directly to the Schrödinger wave equation.

The Peltier effect — where an electric current across a junction of two different conductors generates or absorbs heat — is exploited in compact solid-state coolers and portable vaccine refrigerators.
The Bernoulli principle — that faster-flowing fluid exerts less pressure — is responsible for aircraft lift, the curve of a cricket ball, and the operation of the carburetor in petrol engines.

The field ion microscope, invented by Erwin Müller in 1951, was the first instrument to image individual atoms; its successor, the atom probe, can identify each atom's element as it is field-evaporated.

Strangeness — a quantum number carried by strange quarks — is conserved in strong and electromagnetic interactions but violated in weak interactions, explaining why strange particles decay relatively slowly.

Alpha decay — the emission of a helium-4 nucleus from a radioactive atom — was explained by George Gamow in 1928 as quantum tunnelling through the nuclear potential barrier, one of the first applications of quantum mechanics to nuclear physics.
The Richter scale for earthquake magnitude is logarithmic; each whole-number increase represents a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and roughly 31.6 times more energy released.

Nanotubes of boron nitride, a structural analogue of carbon nanotubes, are electrically insulating and thermally conducting — the opposite of most materials — making them ideal for electrically isolating heat sinks.
The accidental discovery of conducting polymers in 1977 — when polyacetylene was inadvertently over-doped with iodine — earned Heeger, MacDiarmid, and Shirakawa the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Baryogenesis — the process that produced more matter than antimatter in the early universe — remains unexplained; the known sources of CP violation are far too small to account for the observed imbalance.
The ultraviolet catastrophe — the failure of classical physics to predict the spectrum of blackbody radiation — was resolved by Planck's quantum hypothesis in 1900, the birth of quantum theory.

Magnetic reconnection — the explosive rearrangement of magnetic field lines in plasma — is responsible for solar flares, geomagnetic storms, and the aurora borealis, releasing stored magnetic energy as kinetic energy and heat.

The Langmuir probe — a small electrode inserted into plasma to measure electron temperature and density — was invented by Irving Langmuir in the 1920s and is still the standard diagnostic in fusion and space plasma research.

Acoustic levitation uses standing sound waves to suspend small objects without contact — including living insects, water droplets, and even small electronic components — used in pharmaceutical manufacturing to prevent contamination.
The viscosity of water decreases by about 2% per degree Celsius rise in temperature; this is why hot water flows faster through pipes, cuts grease more effectively, and makes tea brew more quickly.

The Jahn-Teller effect — the spontaneous distortion of a symmetric molecule to remove the degeneracy of electronic orbitals — drives the structure of many transition-metal complexes and is central to understanding colossal magnetoresistance in manganites.

The Ising model (1925) is the simplest mathematical model of ferromagnetism; though Ising himself proved it had no phase transition in one dimension, the 2D solution by Onsager in 1944 became a landmark of statistical mechanics.
Electric eels can generate discharges of up to 860 volts — enough to stun a horse — by stacking hundreds of electrocyte cells in series, each acting like a biological battery cell.

The Mpemba discovery inspired a surge of rigorous research; a 2022 study found that certain quantum systems also exhibit Mpemba-like effects in their approach to equilibrium, extending the phenomenon beyond classical thermodynamics.

The Penning trap — an ion trap using crossed magnetic and electric fields — can store single antiprotons and antihydrogen atoms for months, enabling precision tests of CPT symmetry between matter and antimatter.
A magnetar — a neutron star with an extraordinarily intense magnetic field of 10¹⁵ gauss — can distort atoms into thin cylinders and is strong enough to affect chemistry from 1,000 km away.
The Franck-Hertz experiment (1914) showed that electrons lose energy only in fixed discrete quanta when colliding with mercury atoms — direct confirmation that atomic energy levels are quantised.

Polaritons — hybrid quasiparticles formed from photons and excitons strongly coupled inside optical microcavities — can form a Bose-Einstein condensate at room temperature, enabling low-threshold laser-like emission.

The Debye-Scherrer powder diffraction method (1916) allows X-ray crystallography on powdered samples rather than single crystals, making it practical for routine materials identification including soil minerals on Mars rovers.
Lightning can reach temperatures of around 30,000 K — five times hotter than the Sun's surface — and carries about one billion volts, with peak currents of 20,000 amperes in the return stroke.

Thermoelectric generators (TEGs) convert heat directly into electricity using the Seebeck effect; NASA's radioisotope thermoelectric generators powered Voyager, Cassini, and Curiosity using decaying plutonium-238.
Microwave ovens were invented accidentally in 1945 when engineer Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he was standing near a magnetron emitting radar waves.

Velcro was inspired by the burrs of burdock seeds that clung to inventor Georges de Mestral's dog's fur in 1941; examination under a microscope revealed tiny hooks — replicated in nylon to create the fastener.

The Manhattan Project produced the first sustained nuclear chain reaction on 2 December 1942 in a squash court under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, using enriched uranium and graphite moderators.

The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet-B and -C radiation; its depletion by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) was discovered by Molina and Rowland in 1974, earning them a share of the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) maps terrain and autonomous vehicle environments by measuring the round-trip time of laser pulses; archaeologists have used airborne LiDAR to discover entire hidden Mayan cities beneath jungle canopies.
The Compton effect (1923) — where X-rays scattered by electrons shift to longer wavelengths — proved that photons carry momentum and behave as particles, cementing the wave-particle duality of light.

Sonography (ultrasound imaging) uses the piezoelectric effect to generate sound pulses in the megahertz range; echoes returning from tissue boundaries are converted back into electrical signals to build an image.

The adiabatic demagnetisation technique cools paramagnetic salts to millikelvin temperatures by slowly removing a magnetic field — the principal cooling method for achieving sub-kelvin temperatures before dilution refrigerators.
Nitinol, a nickel-titanium shape-memory alloy, remembers its original shape and returns to it when heated; it is used in self-expanding stents, orthodontic wires, and eyeglass frames.

Aerogels — the world's lightest solid materials, made by removing liquid from a gel without collapsing its structure — are 99.98% air by volume and are used as thermal insulation in NASA Mars rover wheels.

Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in nonlinear crystals splits a single photon into two entangled daughter photons; it is the workhorse source of entangled photon pairs for quantum cryptography and computing experiments.

The Mpemba question was the subject of a 2016 Royal Society of Chemistry prize challenge; submitted by over 22,000 participants worldwide, it showed that evaporation and dissolved gases are key, but no single mechanism fully explains all observations.

Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) — sound waves travelling along a piezoelectric surface — are used in mobile phone RF filters to select specific frequency bands, with over 4 billion SAW devices produced annually.

The citizen science project eBird, run by Cornell Lab of Ornithology, has collected over 1 billion bird observations from millions of volunteers, enabling real-time tracking of migratory routes and population trends.

Electric discharge machining (EDM) uses rapid spark erosion to cut any electrically conductive material — including hardened steel and titanium — with micrometre precision and no mechanical cutting force.

Neutron activation analysis bombards a sample with neutrons, turning stable elements into radioactive isotopes whose gamma-ray fingerprints identify every element simultaneously — used to authenticate Old Master paintings and ancient coins.

Friction between tectonic plates stores elastic strain energy for centuries before releasing it in seconds as earthquakes; the seismological study of this cycle is called the elastic rebound theory, formulated by H.F. Reid after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

The dynamo theory explains Earth's magnetic field as generated by convective flow of liquid iron in the outer core; computer simulations show that field reversals happen irregularly, averaging every 300,000 years.

Friction-stir welding, invented in 1991, joins metals by rotating a hard pin tool that plasticises — but never melts — the material; the solid-state process produces stronger, lower-defect welds than fusion welding and is used on the Space Launch System.

Metamaterial cloaking devices bend electromagnetic waves around an object, rendering it invisible at specific wavelengths; the first working microwave cloak was demonstrated at Duke University in 2006.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) mapped over one third of the sky and catalogued 500 million celestial objects, involving over 1,000 scientists and enabling citizen-science spin-offs like Galaxy Zoo.

Quantum chromodynamics predicts 'colour confinement': free quarks can never be observed because the gluon field between separating quarks stores so much energy that a quark-antiquark pair is created before they separate.

Spintronics exploits electron spin in addition to charge; the giant magnetoresistance (GMR) effect — used in every modern hard-disk read head — was discovered independently by Fert and Grünberg in 1988, earning them the 2007 Nobel Prize.

Bioluminescence in deep-sea organisms is so prevalent that over 76% of deep-sea animals emit light; most use it for camouflage, communication, or luring prey in an environment where sunlight never reaches.

In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration produced the first image of a black hole's shadow — the supermassive black hole M87* — using eight radio telescopes across four continents acting as a single Earth-sized dish.

Protein folding misregulation causes amyloid diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, where proteins misfold into beta-sheet fibrils that aggregate; understanding the energy landscape of folding is a frontier of biophysics.

The tribological phenomenon of 'superlubricity' — near-zero friction between incommensurate crystal lattices — was first observed in graphite in 1990 and has been achieved macroscopically with graphene flakes, promising frictionless bearings.

Helioseismology analyses acoustic oscillations of the Sun's surface to infer conditions deep in its interior, just as seismology probes Earth's layers; it has measured the Sun's internal rotation profile with remarkable precision.

Laser cooling, invented in the 1980s, uses the momentum of photons to slow atoms and cool them to microkelvin temperatures; Chu, Cohen-Tannoudji, and Phillips shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics for the technique.

The twin paradox in special relativity — where a twin who travels at near-light speed returns younger than the stay-at-home twin — is not a true paradox; it is confirmed by atomic clocks flown around the world, which run slightly slower than ground clocks.

Gravitational waves, first detected by LIGO in September 2015 from merging black holes 1.3 billion light-years away, stretched and compressed spacetime by less than 1/1000 the diameter of a proton at LIGO's mirrors.

The scanning electron microscope (SEM) uses focused electron beams to generate images with nanometre resolution and three-dimensional surface detail; it transformed materials science, biology, and semiconductor manufacturing after its commercialisation in 1965.

Atomic force microscopy (AFM) measures forces between a sharp tip and a sample surface as the tip scans over it; it can image biological molecules in liquid, measure molecular bonds, and even write with molecules.

Phase-contrast microscopy, developed by Frits Zernike in 1934, converts phase differences in transparent samples into visible contrast, making unstained living cells visible — earning Zernike the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Stimulated emission of radiation — the physical basis of lasers — was predicted by Einstein in 1917 when he showed that a photon could stimulate an excited atom to emit an identical photon; the first working laser was demonstrated by Theodore Maiman in 1960.

Synchrotron self-emission from relativistic electrons spiralling in magnetic fields produces polarised X-rays across the universe; mapping this emission reveals cosmic magnetic field structures in galaxies and galaxy clusters.

The Szilárd engine — a thought experiment proposed by Leo Szilárd in 1929 — explored how information about a single molecule's position could be converted into work, linking information theory with thermodynamics and foreshadowing Landauer's principle.

Landauer's principle (1961) states that erasing one bit of information releases at least kT·ln(2) joules as heat, establishing a fundamental thermodynamic cost to computation that quantum computing researchers try to approach.

Maxwell's demon — a thought experiment proposed in 1871 — imagined a tiny creature sorting fast and slow molecules to decrease entropy; its resolution required the inclusion of information erasure, uniting thermodynamics and information theory.

Inertial confinement fusion (ICF) at the National Ignition Facility achieved scientific ignition in December 2022, releasing more energy from fusion than the laser energy delivered to the target — a historic first.

Neutrino detectors must be buried deep underground to shield against cosmic-ray background; the IceCube detector at the South Pole uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice instrumented with 5,160 optical sensors.
The Weinberg-Salam electroweak theory unified electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force into a single 'electroweak' force at high energies, predicting the W and Z bosons confirmed at CERN in 1983.

The fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137 governs the strength of the electromagnetic force; Pauli was said to be so obsessed with this 'magic number' that he asked God about it after death — it remains dimensionless and inexplicable from first principles.

Gravitational potential energy decreases as objects fall together; the energy released when two black holes merge was detected as a gravitational wave chirp lasting just 0.2 seconds but representing more power than all the stars in the observable universe combined.

The Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems proved that singularities — regions of infinite curvature — are inevitable inside black holes and at the Big Bang, given general relativity holds and energy conditions are satisfied.

The Doppler effect causes a source's observed frequency to shift higher as it approaches and lower as it recedes; Doppler radar in weather forecasting measures the velocity of raindrops toward or away from the antenna.
